name: La Virreina Centre de la Imatge
funding: Ajuntament de Barcelona (Barcelona City Council Institute of Culture - ICUB).
watch: Public visual culture centre in an 18th-century Baroque palace on La Rambla. Directed by writer and curator Valentín Roma.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Centre for the image (Centre de la Imatge) at La Rambla 99, in the Palau de la Virreina, with the Barcelona City Council logo on its website (La Virreina website).

Its exhibition halls host a multidisciplinary project that aims to place cultural policies at the centre of its exhibition activity. The palace is also the headquarters of the Barcelona Institute of Culture (Amics de la Rambla).

Its director Valentín Roma was appointed director of the MACBA unanimously by the general council of the museum consortium on 10 June 2026. He is to start there in the coming weeks (Ara, Antoni Ribas Tur, 10 June 2026, "Valentín Roma es el nuevo director del Macba").

Named for the palace, which took its name from the viceroy's widow, Maria Francesca de Fivaller-Clasquerí i de Bru, who lived there after the death of her husband, Manuel d'Amat, Viceroy of Peru, in 1782 (Catalan Wikipedia).

Building: a baroque and rococo palace built from 1772 for Manuel d'Amat (English Wikipedia). Catalan Wikipedia names Josep Ausich i Mir as the architect and English Wikipedia names Carles Grau. Barcelona City Council bought it in 1944, and it was declared a monument of national interest in 1941 (Catalan Wikipedia).

Earlier uses: first exhibition in 1940 (Amics de la Rambla), the Museu d'Arts Decoratives from 1949 (Catalan Wikipedia), and the City Council's Department of Culture from 1986 (Amics de la Rambla). It also houses the Gabinet Numismàtic de Catalunya and the Museu Postal (Catalan Wikipedia).

Visiting: free admission. Open Tuesday to Sunday and public holidays, 11 am to 8 pm. Closed on 1 and 6 January, 1 May, 24 June, and 25 and 26 December. Groups of more than 10 people book in advance (La Virreina website).
details.funding_verdict: La Virreina Centre de la Imatge: public: Barcelona City Council
funding: Barcelona City Council has owned the palace since 1944 (Catalan Wikipedia), and the centre's website is on the City Council's own domain, ajuntament.barcelona.cat, with the City Council logo (La Virreina website).
The palace is the headquarters of the Barcelona Institute of Culture, the City Council's culture institute (ICUB) (Amics de la Rambla; English Wikipedia).
details.bottom_line: The funder is Barcelona City Council, which owns the building; the palace is the headquarters of the City Council's culture institute, ICUB. Admission is free.

name: Teatro Español
funding: The site carries the Ayuntamiento de Madrid logo and a Madrid Destino Cultura Turismo y Negocio, S.A. footer, and tickets link to a Madrid Destino store. The pages read did not state amounts.
watch: Madrid municipal theatre on Calle del Príncipe, tied to the city council and its company Madrid Destino.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The pages read did not link published accounts.

overview: Theatre at Calle del Príncipe 25, 28012 Madrid (theatre website).
The site links a history page and a publications page; the pages read did not describe its holdings or an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Teatro Español: municipal; amounts not stated on the pages read
funding: Ayuntamiento de Madrid and its company Madrid Destino are named on the site; no amounts are stated (theatre website).
No reporting found of sponsors or income in the pages read.
details.bottom_line: The pages read tie the theatre to the city council and Madrid Destino but give no figures; Madrid Destino's accounts are the next pages to read.

name: Lunds Konsthall
funding: Municipal kunsthalle run by Lund municipality.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: No records of its own. Its parent Lund municipality posts annual reports 2024 and 2025 and lists its culture committee.
affiliations_note: A municipal konsthall that works regularly with Skissernas Museum, Kulturen i Lund and Galleri Aura, and is supported by the independent association Lunds konsthalls vänner.

overview: Municipal art hall at Mårtenstorget 3 in Lund, "part of Lunds kommun" (the hall's website, title translated).
Opened on 21 September 1957 with the exhibition "Svensk nutidskonst". It mainly shows Swedish and Nordic contemporary art, with one or more international exhibitions most years (Swedish Wikipedia).
Designed by architect Klas Anshelm, with high and low rooms, separate spaces for sculpture and large paintings, and open balconies (Swedish Wikipedia).
Gamla Sparbanken, a savings bank, donated the money for the building to the city of Lund. The bank set up a foundation in 1931 to create a concert hall and art salon in Lund (Swedish Wikipedia).
Swedish Wikipedia lists Åsa Nacking as director from 2003.
Open Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday 12:00 to 17:00 and Thursday 12:00 to 20:00. Closed Monday (the hall's website).
funding: The hall's website states that it is part of Lunds kommun; Swedish Wikipedia calls it a municipal art hall.

Lund's Board of Culture and Leisure took the December 2015 decision on the hall's future. Kunstkritikk reports that a conservative minority with support from the Sweden Democrats intended to save 3 million Swedish kronor from the budget; board chairman Joakim Friberg (Social Democrat) claims the reconstruction is unrelated to the savings of around 3 million kronor (Frida Sandström, 17 December 2015).

red_flags.heading: 2015 protest over the municipal decision to reconstruct the hall
points: The protest was aimed at the hall's own owner: the Board of Culture and Leisure of the City of Lund, which runs the hall. Swedish Wikipedia states that on 10 December 2015 the board voted to close the hall with the aim of reopening it later in reconstructed form.
Kunstkritikk reports that the board announced the hall would be "reconstructed" to suit "the present and future Lund", which critics read as a shutdown (Frida Sandström, 17 December 2015).

Director Åsa Nacking said: "An artspace with sixty years of history is being shut down without discussion. The staff and myself are shocked." The artist Matts Leiderstam called the decision another attempt by the board to get rid of Nacking (Kunstkritikk).

An open letter signed by museum directors, university professors and deans appeared in Sydsvenska Dagbladet on 15 December 2015 and was posted on e-flux on 16 December, translated by Anders Kreuger. It calls the plan a "hurried decision" and says the City of Lund "would commit a serious error" (e-flux).

Board vice chairman Peter Bergwall (Green Party) said he could not understand how the director saw the decision as a shutdown (Kunstkritikk, 17 December 2015). Kreuger wrote on 3 February 2016 that the politicians said they never meant to close the hall and planned to hire an outside consultant to study how it could reach more target groups (Kunstkritikk).

press.overall: The three pieces date from 2015 and 2016 and are aimed at the municipal board's decision on the hall.

items.title: Frida Sandström, "The End of Lund's Konsthall as We Know It" (17 December 2015)
points: Reports that Nacking said the decision was made without prior communication, a point Bergwall disputes, and quotes Kreuger and the artist Matts Leiderstam on it; Leiderstam calls it another attempt to get rid of Nacking.
Quotes Bergwall and Friberg; it could not reach Director of Culture Chris Schenlaer.

items.title: "An open letter in support of Lunds konsthall" (16 December 2015, first published in Sydsvenska Dagbladet on 15 December; translated by Anders Kreuger)
points: Ten signatory entries, museum directors, academics and an art academy dean among them, call the decision unfortunate for both the cultural field and democracy, and say there should be investment in professional development instead of discontinuing activities.
Links the decision to the government's October report on museums, which proposes keeping museums "at an arm's length" from political power.

items.title: Anders Kreuger, "Lund's Konsthall: Time and Again" (3 February 2016)
points: Argues the conflict is political, between visual art's demand for autonomy and "cultural animation" aimed at lowering the threshold for everyone.
Describes Nacking as a "seasoned institutional practitioner" with a "critically acclaimed exhibition program" and says the conflict is political, not about her competence.

details.bottom_line: The money behind Lunds Konsthall is municipal: Lund municipality owns and runs it, from a building paid for by a savings bank's donation. The documented issue is the 2015 protest against the municipal board's decision to reconstruct the hall.

name: Malmö Konsthall
funding: Municipal kunsthalle run by the City of Malmö.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: No records of its own. Parent Malmö stad posts its 2025 annual report with accounts.
affiliations_note: Part of the City of Malmö's culture department; it runs Studio KOAS for artists with disabilities, and Skånes Konstförening's members started the 1931 foundation behind the gallery.

overview: Municipal contemporary art hall at S:t Johannesgatan 7, Malmö. It describes itself as part of Malmö stad and sits within the city's Kulturförvaltning (culture administration) (Malmö Konsthall website).
Opened on 22 March 1975. Discussions about a dedicated contemporary art space in Malmö had run since the 1930s (Malmö Konsthall, "50 years" page).

Designed by the Lund architect Klas Anshelm (1914 to 1980), with a glass facade facing Magistratsparken, a large north-facing skylight and 526 lanterns with individually adjustable light (Malmö Konsthall, "50 years" page). Wikipedia says it was built from 1971 to 1974 in concrete, glass, wood and aluminium and won the 1974 Kasper Salin Prize.
A 1994 renovation connected it to the neighbouring brick Hantverkshuset, adding a bookshop, a children's area and a restaurant (Wikipedia).

No permanent collection. About 2,000 square metres of exhibition space, which the Konsthall calls "basically just a white box" (Malmö Konsthall website). It has staged close to 600 exhibitions and three large ones a year (Malmö Konsthall website).

Artistic directors: Eje Högestätt 1975 to 1986, Björn Springfeldt 1986 to 1990, Sune Nordgren 1990 to 1996, Bera Nordal 1997 to 2002, Lars Grambye 2003 to 2007, Jacob Fabricius 2007 to 2013, Diana Baldon 2014 to 2016, and Mats Stjernstedt from 2017 (Malmö Konsthall, "50 years" page). Malmö stad announced Stjernstedt's appointment on 12 September 2016, with Culture Director Elisabeth Lundgren quoted.
On site: the restaurant SMAK, a bookshop, the children's workshop Verkstan and the youth programme Malmö Konsthall U (Malmö Konsthall website).
Admission is free. Open Tuesday to Sunday, closed on Mondays and major holidays. The site links an accessibility statement (Malmö Konsthall website).
details.funding_verdict: Malmö Konsthall: public: a unit of the City of Malmö's culture administration
funding: The Konsthall is part of Malmö stad's Kulturförvaltning (Malmö Konsthall website). Culture Director Elisabeth Lundgren gave the city's reasons for appointing Mats Stjernstedt as its head in 2016 (Malmö stad, 12 September 2016).
Admission to exhibitions and programmes is free (Malmö Konsthall website).
details.bottom_line: The Konsthall is run by the City of Malmö as part of its culture administration, and entry is free. Its funding is municipal.

name: Fondation Pierre Gianadda
funding: A private foundation created by the engineer Léonard Gianadda after his brother Pierre died in 1976. The pages read did not state its budget or funders; its site lists three bodies, the Fondation Pierre Gianadda, the Fondation Annette et Léonard Gianadda and the Fondation Léonard Gianadda Mécénat, and an Amis de la Fondation membership.
watch: Léonard Gianadda died on 3 December 2023 aged 88; the pages read did not say who runs the foundation now.
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts.

overview: The Fondation Pierre Gianadda is a museum and cultural centre at Rue du Forum 59 in Martigny, Valais, with a Gallo-Roman museum, an automobile museum and a sculpture park (foundation website).

The museum opened on 19 November 1978; Léonard Gianadda, a photojournalist in the 1950s and a civil engineer who opened an office in Martigny in 1961, created the foundation after his brother Pierre died in a plane crash in 1976 (swissinfo).

What is there: ruins of a Gallo-Roman temple found on the site, shown in the central space; about 50 vintage cars from 1897 to 1939 in the basement; and, since the 1990s, 47 outdoor sculptures owned by the foundation in the park, including works by Bourdelle, Maillol, Rodin, Arp, Moore, Miró and Calder (Universalis).
Over 45 years it hosted 180 exhibitions with nearly 11 million visitors and 46 music seasons (swissinfo). The current exhibition is 'Rodin selon Rilke' (foundation website).
Archive: the site holds an archive of its exhibitions from 1978 to 2017 (foundation website).
details.funding_verdict: Fondation Pierre Gianadda: private foundation; funders and budget not stated on the pages read
funding: No reporting found on the pages read of the foundation's budget, public grants or sponsors; the site's 'Partenaires' section was linked but did not name partners on the page read.
Founder: Léonard Gianadda founded it in memory of his brother; the site presents him as the visionary behind it.
details.bottom_line: A founder-led private foundation. The pages read show the structure of three foundations but no money figures; no 2018 closure reporting or succession dispute was found.

name: Museum Rietberg
funding: The museum's site links to a City of Zurich culture page for it; the pages read did not state who funds it or give amounts.
watch: On 20 March 2026 the city transferred ownership of 11 Benin objects held at the museum to Nigeria; the museum led the Benin Initiative Schweiz, which examined 96 artefacts in Swiss collections.
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts.

overview: The Museum Rietberg is a museum of non-European art at Gablerstrasse 15 in Zurich; its tagline is 'World Art in Zurich' (museum website).
The pages read did not state its founder or opening year.
What is there: the pages read gave no collection size; they describe Benin works among its holdings, 11 of which were transferred to Nigeria in 2026 (SRF, 20 March 2026).
Archive: the pages read did not describe a library or archive.
details.funding_verdict: Museum Rietberg: public, tied to the City of Zurich; amounts not stated on the pages read
funding: City of Zurich: the museum's footer links to the city's culture page for it; no grant figure on the pages read.
No reporting found of private donors or sponsors on the pages read.

red_flags.heading: Looted or contested holdings: Benin works
points: On 20 March 2026 the cities of Zurich and Geneva signed in Zurich's Rathaus the transfer of ownership of 28 Benin objects to Nigeria: 11 from the Museum Rietberg, 14 from the University of Zurich's Völkerkundemuseum and 3 from Geneva's Musée d'ethnographie; 27 more held in Basel, Neuchâtel and St. Gallen were still pending (SRF, 20 March 2026).
Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments (NCMM) filed a formal request in July 2024 on behalf of Nigeria and the Kingdom of Benin (Finestre sull'Arte, 23 March 2026).
The Benin Initiative Schweiz examined 96 artefacts from 2021 to 2024 and found 55 likely came from the 1897 looting (SRF).

Esther Tisa, head of provenance research at the Rietberg and co-leader of the initiative, said the aim was to make amends for the injustice and that most works are planned to be publicly accessible; NCMM director-general Olugbile Holloway said the return can help 'heal some of the rifts inherited from the colonial period' (SRF; Finestre sull'Arte). Some objects stay in Switzerland on loan; the rest go to Nigeria in summer 2026.

details.bottom_line: The museum belongs to the city and the pages read give no money figures. The contested matter, the Benin objects, ended in a transfer of ownership to Nigeria in March 2026.

name: National Museum of Damascus
funding: Its parent body, the Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums, partners UNESCO's 2025 project: initial budget $175,000, no donor named.
watch: Closed 7 December 2024 after the fall of Damascus and reopened 8 January 2025. Wikipedia reports six Roman statues stolen in a November 2025 break-in.
records_note: The parent Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums publishes no annual reports, accounts, donors or board; it is tied to the Minister of Culture.

overview: National museum of Syrian archaeology on Shukri al-Quwatli Street, west of the city centre, between Damascus University and the Sulaymaniyya Takiyya (Wikipedia).
Founded in 1919 under the Syrian Ministry of Education at Al-Adiliyah Madrasa. Wikipedia calls it the oldest cultural heritage institution in Syria.

The present building was completed in 1936 beside the Sulaymaniyya Takiyya, and its facade uses the front walls of the Umayyad palace Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi, moved from the Syrian Desert. The official opening was in 1950, with later additions in 1953, 1963, 1974 and 2004 (Wikipedia).

Holds more than 300,000 items covering more than 11 millennia, including over 5,000 cuneiform tablets, the Ugaritic alphabet, the Dura-Europos synagogue wall paintings, the Hypogeum of Yarhai and the Lion of al-Lat (Wikipedia).

It closed in 2012 during the civil war, when staff hid its artefacts, and partly reopened in late October 2018. Wikipedia says four of its five wings reopened on 29 October 2018 (Smithsonian Magazine, Brigit Katz, 30 October 2018; Wikipedia).

Wikipedia says it closed again on 7 December 2024 after the fall of Damascus and that the Directorate-General requested security from Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. The Associated Press (11 November 2025) reports it reopened on 8 January 2025.

On the night of 9 November 2025 thieves broke into the classical department. An anonymous official told the Associated Press six marble Roman-era statues were taken. The Directorate-General said "some exhibits" were missing and opened an investigation, and the police chief, Brig. Gen. Osama Atkeh, told the state news agency SANA that guards and other people were being questioned (Associated Press, Gaith Alsayed, 11 November 2025).
details.funding_verdict: National Museum of Damascus: Syria's Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums, with a UNESCO emergency project from 2025
funding: The Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums is the museum's partner in the UNESCO project and requested security for the museum in December 2024 (Wikipedia).

In June 2025 UNESCO launched a first-aid project with the Directorate-General for the museum, with an initial budget of $175,000 covering emergency preparedness, restoration of damaged objects, digitisation of documentary heritage and staff training in inventory, museology and heritage education (Finestre sull'Arte, Noemi Capoccia, 14 June 2025; North Press, 11 June 2025). Finestre sull'Arte mentions "new financial commitments" from international partners.
details.bottom_line: The museum works with Syria's Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums, which partnered with UNESCO on an emergency project with an initial budget of $175,000 launched in June 2025. The documented events are the closure and reopening around the fall of the Assad government and the November 2025 theft of six Roman statues.

name: Tishreen War Panorama (October War Panorama)
funding: Run by the Syrian Ministry of Defence, which lists it among its army museums. North Korea helped build it, per Wikipedia and Public Delivery.
watch: Wikipedia, citing a visit video, says it was ransacked after December 2024. Opening is dated 1998 (Wikipedia) and 9 October 1999 (Frontline Club).
affiliations_note: Part of the Syrian Ministry of Defence's military culture and museums section.

propaganda.summary: Syrian state war museum opened October 1999 under Hafez al-Assad, its panorama painted by North Korea's Mansudae Overseas Development Group. It presents the 1973 Quneitra assault as heroic victory and displays murals of Assad.

overview: War museum at the northern entrance of Damascus, in a garden of about 62,700 square metres (Syrian Ministry of Defence page in Arabic, archived 2018, translated here).
Commemorates the 1973 October War from a Syrian viewpoint, and battles of the 1982 Lebanon War (Wikipedia).
Opening is dated 1998, inaugurated by Hafez al-Assad (Wikipedia), and 9 October 1999 (Frontline Club visitor).
Built with North Korean help (Wikipedia; Frontline Club). Wikipedia points to socialist-realist reliefs and a mural of Hafez al-Assad with Kim Il Sung.

Ministry page: a domed hall 43.1 metres across and 37.1 metres high. A circular painted panorama 130 metres long and 15 metres high shows the Golan Heights. Two weapons yards of 1,760 square metres each hold Syrian equipment in one and Israeli equipment in the other.
A visitor describes a short film, a rotating platform in front of a 360-degree painting of Quneitra, and an outdoor display of Syrian and Israeli hardware (Frontline Club).
Unverified: Wikipedia, citing a video of a visit, says people ransacked and destroyed parts of the building after the fall of the Assad government.
details.funding_verdict: Tishreen War Panorama: public: Syrian Ministry of Defence
funding: The Ministry of Defence runs the museum and lists it under museums in the culture section of its website; the page describes the building and exhibits.

North Korea helped build it (Wikipedia; Frontline Club). Public Delivery says Mansudae Overseas Projects helped build it. The EU's 2017 listing of Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies lists Syria among the countries where the group "has been reported to conduct business" (Implementing Regulation 2017/1457).

press.overall: One visitor's blog post discusses the museum. It is not an art review, and it criticises the presentation, not the funding.

items.title: unsigned blog post by a student visitor, "Winning a battle, losing the war: an odd tribute" (undated)
points: Says the museum celebrates a war that was far from victorious and dwells on the storming of Quneitra, although Israel retook the town.
Calls the 360-degree painting impressive and credits the North Korean artists.
Says the building was constructed with help from North Korea.

details.bottom_line: The museum belongs to the Syrian Ministry of Defence, and no flagged funder was found in the sources opened. Wikipedia, Public Delivery and one visitor's account describe the North Korean role. Worth watching: the building's condition after the change of government, and whether the Ministry's page, now down, is restored.

name: National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts
funding: Funded by the Ministry of Culture. 2025 gifts of NT$5.64M came from property and building-materials firms, the E.SUN Foundation (bank) and individuals.
watch: The filing masks some donor names. In Aug 2026 the Gwangju Biennale renamed its Taiwan Pavilion 'NTMoFA', a row the museum did not cause.
records_note: Annual reports 2017 to 2025, audited final accounts and dated donation lists are on its site.
finances_note: FY2025 income about NT$700M: about 97 percent central government transfers, 2.5 percent earned from fees, concession royalties and course fees; donated property is excluded (final accounts 2025, p. 102).
affiliations_note: Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

overview: State art museum in Taichung, known as NTMoFA (Wikipedia).

Opened on 26 June 1988 under the Taiwan Provincial Government's education department, originally as the Museum of Art. It closed in 1999 for earthquake-damage renovation and reopened in July 2004 (Wikipedia).
Placed under the Council of Cultural Affairs, which Wikipedia says was restructured as the Ministry of Culture on 20 May 2012.
The main building has four storeys, about 37,953 square metres of building area and a 102,000 square metre outdoor courtyard, with 16 galleries (Wikipedia).
Outdoor features include a sculpture park of 45 sculptures and a forest of 50 calligraphy stone tablets (Wikipedia).
It has organised Taiwan's pavilion at the Venice Architecture Biennale since 2000 and runs the International Biennial Print Exhibition and the Taiwan Biennial (Wikipedia).
Closed Mondays. The main building opens Tuesday to Friday 12:00 to 18:00, Saturday 10:00 to 20:00 and Sunday 10:00 to 18:00. Admission is free except for special exhibitions (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts: mainly public: Taiwan's Ministry of Culture
funding: The museum is a Ministry of Culture institution (Wikipedia).
The museum's donations page lists reports on donations received from outside bodies from 2016 to the January to June 2026 report, dated 25 August 2026 (museum website).
wider_context: August 2026 naming dispute at the 16th Gwangju Biennale: a biennale poster listed Taiwan's satellite exhibition as the "NTMoFA Pavilion". Curator Chen Xiang-Wen and nine artists objected on 15 August, saying the name was changed without their consent and "brutally erased Taiwan from the poster" (The Art Newspaper, Lisa Movius, 26 August 2026).

The Gwangju Biennale Foundation said a 12 January 2026 agreement set the museum-based name, because the pavilion was an institutional one. Taiwan's Ministry of Culture said it was agreed as the "Taiwan Pavilion" under an agreement signed on 2 April. On 25 August, after agreeing with the ministry, the foundation approved the name "Taiwan Pavilion" (The Art Newspaper).

ArtReview (staff report, 26 August 2026) reports that the pavilion's artists and curators, the ministry and a letter signed by twenty other contributors called the change "political censorship". The organisers called the listing an "administrative convention" and said the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts signed the agreement as an institutional participant, not a national one.

The Art Newspaper reports that Chen suggested pressure from larger forces behind the scenes, with no evidence that the Chinese or South Korean governments were involved; the foundation said it did not intervene in or censor the exhibition's content. The objection was aimed at the Gwangju Biennale Foundation, not the museum.

Central News Agency (udn, 24 August 2026) reported that 21 Gwangju art organisations signed a joint statement supporting Taiwan and aimed at the biennale organisation, whose decision-making it questioned.

The connection to the museum: according to the artists' statement quoted by The Art Newspaper, the museum submitted the proposal under the Taiwan Pavilion name; the organisers say it signed the agreement as an institutional participant, and its acronym was used for the pavilion.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is Taiwan's public budget through the Ministry of Culture, with outside donations reported in dated lists on its site. Nothing in the sources links a flagged funder to the museum. The 2026 Gwangju row was aimed at the biennale foundation's labelling of the pavilion; the museum was the named institutional participant.

name: National Museum of Tajikistan
watch: Established 1934; renamed National Museum of Tajikistan in 2011 and moved into a new building in March 2013 with 22 halls and over 50,000 objects.
records_note: No museum site loaded; a government portal shows it is a state institution under the president's office.

overview: National history and art museum on Ismoil Somoni Street, next to State Flag Square in central Dushanbe (Eurasia.Travel).

Founded in 1934 with 530 items from the Tajik SSR Academy of Sciences and expeditions. It was formerly named for the Persian miniaturist Kamoliddin Behzad, was renamed the National Museum of Tajikistan in 2011 and moved to its present building in March 2013 (Eurasia.Travel).

The earlier museum, the Behzod museum, was founded by a decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee in 1934 on the basis of an exhibition of economic achievements, held national status from 1999 by government decision, and worked in a former technical college building at 31 Aini Street (Orexca, an older description).
The present building has 22 exhibition halls over 15,000 square metres, and Wikipedia gives a total area of 24,000 square metres (Eurasia.Travel; Wikipedia).

Four departments: natural history, ancient and medieval history, modern and contemporary history, and fine and applied arts (Wikipedia). Research departments cover written heritage, archaeology and numismatics (Eurasia.Travel).

Over 50,000 objects from the Bronze Age to the early 20th century, including Samanid coins, Sogdian pottery, material from the Sogdian castle on Mount Mug, the 11th to 12th century Iskandar mihrab and a large clay Buddha from the Ajina-Tepa temple restored by a team from the Hermitage Museum (Eurasia.Travel). Hellenistic sculptures from Takht-i Sangin are in the displays (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: National Museum of Tajikistan: state museum under the Ministry of Culture
funding: Orexca, in an older description of the earlier Behzod museum, says that since its founding the museum has been under the Ministry of Culture of Tajikistan.
Unverified: a Koryo Group travel blog says the museum was built in 2011 by order of President Emomali Rahmon; Eurasia.Travel says the museum moved into its present building in March 2013.
details.bottom_line: The museum is a state institution under Tajikistan's Ministry of Culture, housed since March 2013 in its present building.
